value.overview: The Mangrove Hummingbird (Chrysuronia boucardi) is a small hummingbird endemic to Costa Rica. It is closely associated with Pacific-coast mangrove forests, especially stands containing piñuela mangrove (Pelliciera rhizophorae). Unlike many hummingbirds with broad habitat use, this species has a highly restricted distribution and depends heavily on coastal wetlands. Its localized range, specialized habitat, and continuing pressure on mangrove ecosystems make it one of Costa Rica’s most distinctive conservation birds.
value.classification: The Mangrove Hummingbird belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the emerald hummingbird group, tribe Trochilini. Recent genetic research supports placement in the genus Chrysuronia; older sources commonly use the name Amazilia boucardi or Polyerata boucardi.
value.identification: Adults are small, compact hummingbirds with bronze-green upperparts. The male has a bright bluish-green throat and breast, white lower belly and undertail coverts, and a dark, shallowly forked tail with narrow outer feathers. Females are duller below, with mostly white underparts marked by bronze-green along the sides; the outer tail feathers have narrow pale tips. Its restricted mangrove habitat and contrasting blue-green throat help distinguish it from other Costa Rican coastal hummingbirds.
value.rangeHabitat: The Mangrove Hummingbird occurs only in Costa Rica, along the Pacific coast from the Gulf of Nicoya southward to the Gulf of Dulce. In Costa Rica it is found in separated mangrove wetlands rather than in a continuous range. It mainly inhabits large, mature mangrove stands, particularly those rich in piñuela mangrove, and may visit nearby forest edges, second growth, clearings, and flowering trees. It is now uncommon in parts of the Gulf of Nicoya and more frequent farther south, including the Gulf of Dulce region.
value.migrationStatus: Resident and apparently sedentary. It is endemic to Costa Rica and does not undertake a known long-distance migration; individuals generally remain in or near Pacific-coast mangrove habitats throughout the year.
value.breeding: The reported breeding season extends approximately from October through February. As in other hummingbirds, the female is expected to build and tend the nest and provide care for the young, while the male contributes little or no parental care. Available information on nest placement, clutch size, incubation, and fledging is limited compared with that for widespread hummingbird species. Breeding habitat is closely linked to intact coastal mangroves and nearby vegetation that supplies flowers and small arthropods.
value.dietFeeding: The species feeds mainly on nectar, especially from flowers of piñuela mangrove. It also visits flowering plants in adjacent habitats, including Inga, Heliconia, Maripa, Lonchocarpus, and some epiphytes. Small insects and other arthropods provide protein, particularly for growth and reproduction. It obtains food by hovering at flowers and may defend productive feeding sites, although its movements are generally concentrated within mangrove forests and nearby coastal vegetation.
value.behavior: The Mangrove Hummingbird is an active, territorial nectar feeder that usually forages within mangrove vegetation or at its edges. It can move into nearby second growth and forest clearings when suitable flowers are available. Its flight includes the rapid hovering typical of hummingbirds, with quick movements between flowers and perches. A soft, rapidly delivered descending twitter or short “djt” note has been reported. Because its habitat is patchy, local movements may follow flowering and water-level conditions.

conservation.populationTrend: The population is considered to be declining, with the main concern being the loss and degradation of its limited mangrove habitat. Distribution is fragmented, and the species is locally uncommon in parts of its range.
conservation.threats: The principal threat is destruction and degradation of Pacific-coast mangroves, including clearing for coastal development, aquaculture, agriculture, infrastructure, and other land uses. Pollution, altered water flow, sedimentation, and disturbance can further reduce habitat quality. Because the species depends strongly on particular mangrove communities and has a small, fragmented range, the loss of individual wetlands may have disproportionate effects.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore Pacific-coast mangrove wetlands, especially mature stands containing piñuela mangrove. Support effective management of protected areas and Ramsar wetlands, maintain natural freshwater and tidal flows, and prevent clearing, pollution, and unplanned coastal development. Conservation programs should monitor populations and breeding sites, preserve habitat corridors between mangrove patches, and involve local communities in sustainable mangrove stewardship.
